utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, I see that you're on your feet. I have a few procedural matters, and if you wouldn't mind it, I would first deal with mine and then -- the first one is that the Chamber still owes you and the public the reasons for granting protective measures to Witness 62 and I will give them now. On the 12th of June, the Chamber granted protective measures for a witness who was given the pseudonym of Witness 62 with reasons to follow. The Trial Chamber hereby gives reasons for its decision. On the 8th of June, 2007, the Prosecution applied for the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face and voice distortion of Witness 62. The witness and his family live in Kosovo. The witness has expressed fear for his safety and that of his extended family, should it become publicly known that he gave evidence for the Prosecution. On the 12th of June, 2007, the Chamber put on the record that the Defence did not oppose the motion. The party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard may be satisfied by demonstrating a combination of the following three factors: One, the witness's testimony may antagonise persons who reside in a specific territory; two, the witness or his or her family live or work in that territory, have property in that territory, or have concrete plans to return to live in that territory; and, three, there exists an unstable security situation in that territory, which is particularly unfavourable to witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. By common agreement in this case, the last of these three factors is not contested. Given the nature of the witness's testimony, the Chamber is satisfied that it may antagonise persons who reside in Witness 62's community. The Chamber notes that the witness and his extended family live in a village in Kosovo, and the witness feels that should it become publicly known that he testified before the Tribunal his family will face retaliation. Therefore, as the Chamber is satisfied that the requirements for granting protective measures are met, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request for pseudonym and face and voice distortion. This concludes the Chamber's reasons for granting protective measures to Witness 62. And I would also like to give the reasons for the decision on the Defence request to defer the issuance of a subpoena for Witness 30. On the 12th of June, I announced that the Chamber was not persuaded by the Defence's argument in support of deferring a decision on the issuance of a subpoena for Witness 30. The subpoena was issued on the same day. The Chamber would now like to briefly explain the reasons for its decision. In its joint submissions of the 6th and the 7th of June, 2007, the Defence argued that the credibility and reliability of Witness 30's expected evidence was such as to call into question the probative value and fairness of the admission of the witness's evidence. It follows in the Defence's argument that a decision on the subpoena for the witness must await the Chamber's decision on whether to permit the Prosecution to call this witness at all. The Defence relies on Rule 89(D), which states that evidence may be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The Defence has raised two disclosure issues relating to Witness 30. The details need not to be summarized here. Suffice it to say, that the Chamber expects the parties to resolve these issues and hopes that it will not be required to intervene further. The Prosecution is urged to respond to the Defence's request as soon as possible if it has not done so already. Nonetheless, the fact that these disclosure issues exist is not a reason for us to defer a decision on the issuance of the requested subpoena. We do not know at this stage that the probative value of Witness 30's evidence is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The Defence argues that there is a possibility that may be realised upon the disclosure of the information that the Defence is seeking to obtain from the Prosecution; however, at this stage it is only a hypothesis. It should be clear from my remarks that our decision does not prohibit the Defence from coming back to us with a further Rule 89(D) motion concerning Witness 30. The fact that the witness has in the meantime been subpoenaed is not an obstacle to that. This concludes the reasons for the Chamber's decision. Then the next issue I would like to deal with is the two Prosecution videos that were attached to forensic reports, portions of which were played. I do understand that it is preferred by the registry that they receive two separate numbers and that they will thus be considered for admission. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I understand -- I understand that's the situation. I ask that they be admitted into evidence. Apparently the video-clip depicting the car upside down in the water is 65 ter 1385, and the video-clip depicting the car right-side up in the water, where you can see its red colour, that is identified as 65 ter 1386. And I would ask that they be given their separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you are referring to these 65 ter numbers, does that mean that the portion that was played is the whole of these 65 ter documents, or 1385 is -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not more, not less than the portion. MR. DI FAZIO: No. Purely and simply those clips. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objection against admission of these two exhibits which have not received yet a number from what I understand, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1385 becomes P349, and 65 ter number 1386 will become P350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the absence of any objections, P349 and P350 are admitted into evidence. On my agenda, the only remaining matter for the moment is something which perhaps should not be raised at this moment by me, but the Chamber is aware that there was -- there is some discussion on the intent, from what I understand, the intent of the Prosecutor for the next witness to seek admission under Rule 92 ter of the statement taken in January of this year. If that comes to us, we'll hear from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's part of what I need to raise with you at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I put the position in context. Your Honours will have, I think, received an application from the Prosecution that was filed yesterday to amend the indictment to insert into Counts 21 and 22, amongst another -- there were two principal amendments. The one that I'm concerned with at the moment is a proposed amendment to Count 21 and 22, adding particulars of an individual who, until now, is asserted to be an unidentified set of remains, but in respect of whom, the motion explains, the International Commission for Missing Persons at the end of May have produced material, which of course the Defence have not had an opportunity to verify, identifying one of those sets of remains as a woman called Sanije Balaj. Now, Your Honour may remember the name from the evidence of Rrustem Tetaj and from the witness statement of Gani Gjukaj which I put to Rrustem Tetaj, essentially confirming both in the witness statement and in the testimony that there was an investigation into the death of this woman which appeared to have been in some way or another connected to a man called Mete Krasniqi at Barane. The position until now has been that that account, that incident, was not a count in the indictment but was part of the general background to the case and was not, therefore, in any sense, a focal point of Defence investigations. The amendment, which of course one understands is an application that follows on from the discovery during the trial of further forensic DNA material, which plainly places the Prosecution in a somewhat different position in respect of that set of remains, but the proposed amendment sets out a detailed account of how the Prosecution alleged this woman met her death. And part of that sequence of events involves the next witness because, as he is now named in the amended count in the indictment, he took part, as he acknowledges himself in his witness statement, in interviewing this woman on the grounds of suspected collaboration prior to releasing her and allowing her to be taken away by three other named individuals who, the Prosecution allege, then drove her to another location and murdered her. The position is that whenever it was the Prosecution became aware of the ICMP's findings - and no doubt Mr. Re will be able to help us with that in a moment or two - the planning of the Prosecution's case and the presentation of this witness's evidence at this time places the Defence in a very, very real difficulty. Just to recap, if I may, briefly. During May, the second half of May, the Prosecution served on the Defence, on the 25th, in fact, of May, two witness statements from cousins of the victim which related certain matters about the supposed circumstances of her death. On the 8th of June, the Prosecution then served upon the Defence a further witness statement from the next witness, which is dated the 15th of May, 2007. And then yesterday, together with the application to amend, the Prosecution served three further witness statements and transcripts of interviews of two witnesses who've given evidence during the course of proceedings currently taking place in Kosovo to prosecute an individual said to have been the actual perpetrator. Now, I, frankly, have not had an opportunity so far to assimilate or master that material, in part because the Prosecution had indicated until today that a different witness was due to testify first, but that is a problem which may be overcomable with a sufficient interval between evidence in-chief and cross-examination. But there's a somewhat more fundamental problem at stake here. As I indicated, an individual by the name of Idriz Gashi is currently the subject of a prosecution in Kosovo. That cross-examination has not concluded in a verdict. Evidence has been taken. We understand from information that we have managed to obtain since receiving the application to amend the indictment - in other words in the last 24 hours - that the case is due to resume on the 22nd of June for closing submissions but those closing submissions have been adjourned in the past on more than one occasion. We do not have access to the file of evidence that was -- has been compiled in the course of that trial. Only one or two statements that have been selected by the Prosecution and appended to its application to amend the indictment, to which of course we have not yet filed any response. And in the midst of that, the Prosecution elects to put this witness on the witness-stand at this point to give evidence about circumstances surrounding the disappearance and death of this woman, for which he was, himself, a suspect. Now, it is plain, in our submission, that the Defence ought not fairly to be put in the position of having to cross-examine this witness about that aspect of his testimony until we are in a position to assimilate the material that has been served and obtain the material that ought to have been served before this could properly be put forward as an application to amend the indictment, and certainly before we could be put in a position of having to cross-examine. I've had an opportunity to discuss the position with Mr. Re just before Your Honours came into court. His suggestion was that in some way the evidence of this witness might be severable; in other words, that he might give evidence in-chief on all aspects but then be cross-examined on matters other than the death of Sanije Balaj and to return, presumably, at a later stage to be cross-examined in that regard. That is not a solution which I would regard as remotely satisfactory because his relationship with the investigation into collaboration investigations of Sanije Balaj is intrinsic to the account he gives of organisation, distribution -- of disciplinary responsibilities in the Barane HQ. In other words, it's inextricably bound up with the general testimony that he gives. I'm sure there are certain aspects of his account which could be severed at the other end, in the sense that they're not inextricably bound up with this part of his testimony, but it's, in our submission, a most unsatisfactory suggestion, given that it arises so late as a result of the Prosecution having made the decision to put this witness in the witness box without notifying in advance the Defence, that is to say, in advance of -- at the time when witness list was being compiled, of the situation that we were likely to find ourselves in. We have, of course, as I indicated, and as the application to amend indicates, been notified that the identification has occurred, that is to say, the ICMP results have occurred. We were notified of that on the 6th of June and that there would be an application to amend the indictment, but the supporting material, as I say, came yesterday, and we have none of the material from the trial, other than the two extracts that have been provided. In practical terms, my suggestion this: That Mr. Re call the witness to give evidence in-chief and then we adjourn this witness's testimony. I will be in a position, I think, by the end of tomorrow to know whether further investigations in Kosovo are going to be essential before cross-examining the witness on this aspect of the account; in other words, how long it is likely to take us to obtain material relating to the ongoing prosecution of Idriz Gashi for perpetrating this particular offence. But it is, we would submit, a strange and unsatisfactory situation to be putting on the witness-stand an individual who is suspected of being a perpetrator but who gives an account exonerating himself at a time when a trial is taking place of somebody who is alleged by the prosecuting authorities in Kosovo to be the perpetrator when that trial hasn't been concluded, and the parties, that is to say the Defence, have not been furnished with the material that's necessary to cross-examine. All of that, as I say, and I don't wish to repeat myself, all of that comes about solely because the Prosecution has chosen the order of witnesses that it has, and I'm, if I may say so, extremely unhappy about that state of affairs. In addition to that, Your Honour referred to some correspondence this morning concerning the possibility of a Rule 92 ter statement. We received from Mr. Re yesterday afternoon an e-mail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you there first. Is my understanding right: That what is proposed to be tendered as 92 ter material does not in any way refer to the -- well, let's say for the time being, for the disappearance of Sanije Balaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question for this reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... the answer is no and I've taken it out. It's not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The answer is no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that my understanding is right that it's not in there. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We don't intend to lead evidence in 92 ter form about Sanije Balaj, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I can just explain, I received an e-mail yesterday evening from Mr. Re indicating that the Prosecution's intention was to seek to rely upon the whole of the January 2007 statement pursuant to the provisions of 92 ter, and that does include reference to Sanije Balaj. I responded this morning by e-mail indicating that there was certain passages in that statement to which I objected in terms of admissibility, whether the evidence was adduced 92 ter or orally. I didn't receive a response --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have on my list that from the Defence until now, that's what I took from the e-mails that have been sent to us, that paragraphs 29, 42, 80, and 81 are at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. The particular passages in the first two paragraphs Your Honour has mentioned are opposed solely on the basis and only to the extent that they contain expressions of opinion on what is a matter of law. But I received no direct response or at least I was not aware of having received a direct response. But shortly before we sat I gather that a further 92 ter statement, different from the one that I was asked to respond to, which not only omits certain matters but includes certain other matters from other statements was apparently circulated. I haven't seen it. I haven't had an opportunity to read or assimilate it, and I understand Mr. Re now wishes to make a 92 ter application in respect of it. I see notes being placed in front of me. It was dispatched at 20 minutes to 2.00 this afternoon. I'm not in a position to respond to that, and I don't expect that I ought to be asked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Re, to respond to what has been raised by Mr. Emmerson, perhaps I would invite other counsel - that's you, Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Troop - to add whatever you would like to add to what Mr. Emmerson said so that we can receive a comprehensive response from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I fully concur with the remarks made by Mr. Emmerson. I have a laundry list of specific list of information that we have not received that I will not read into the record because I think at this point in time it would not necessarily be the most fruitful use of time. Needless to say, there are quite a number of items that we do not have as a result of a review of the motion to amend the indictment and nothing more. In addition, we have been, as you know, for some period of time attempting to get UNMIK information and other information concerning a number of investigations that were extant in Kosovo, and specifically this investigation, the investigation concerning the circumstances surrounding Sanije Balaj. We were informed today through conversation with UNMIK that any information they have they will not be able to get to us before the 20th of June. They will give us an interim response to our request sometime before that. This particular request has been an outstanding request before the hearing on May 10th and remains truly a problematic situation. I am certainly not in a position, in any sense whatsoever, and especially in light of the manner in which the Prosecution has chosen to proceed to attempt to amend the indictment. I am not in a position whatsoever at this point in time to review, assimilate, and appropriately represent my client from the standpoint of a cross-examination at this juncture. It would be, as a matter of fact, as far as I'm concerned, irresponsible on my part to proceed. I am extremely troubled by the order of witness calling, and specifically the fact that this particular witness has been called at this time because he is a central witness to issues concerning not only what is becoming clearly a live issue in this trial, that of collaboration, but also his own personal involvement, and we do not even have at this time the entirety of a trial record wherein many facts that I think would shed light on the facts and circumstances concerning this entire matter have been completed. In addition, for purposes of clarity, I believe that paragraph 24 of the 92 ter statement - and I'm moving to that for a minute - mentions Sanije Balaj's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise, I did inadvertently mislead the Court there. That is why I wished to rise before I had re-checked it. In paragraph 24 there is a brief reference but it's a fairly harmless one. There is a reference in paragraph 85 which I thought had been taken out but hasn't. It said: "In the case of Sanije Balaj there was an unfortunate was execution without a fair trial. Such things are not supposed to happen." I won't leave that under 92 ter; I'll take that out. But I apologise. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd take out both the references?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, the first one in paragraph 24 just simply says: "The former police inspector Hasan Gashi became their commander. He was stationed his troops in the red school where Sanije Balaj was brought." In my submission, that's fairly harmless and doesn't go to culpability.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The test is not only whether it's harmless but also whether it has probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I simply say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At the moment, I don't understand Mr. Re to be suggesting, and perhaps he can clarify if this is the suggestion, that he intends not to elicit testimony about Sanije Balaj. My understanding is that if it's the Prosecution's intention to elicit oral testimony in-chief about Sanije Balaj, and if that is the case, then whether it's in the 92 ter statements or not is really secondary to the fact that the Prosecution would be aiming to elicit that evidence as part of its case, and therefore the Defence is not in a position to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, I'm trying to find the harmless passage, that is -- should be the interview, 7th and 9th of January of this year, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... it's paragraph 24 of the 92 ter -- proposed 92 ter statement. I have hard copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When have you sent that to --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That was included in the one I sent last night, and the revised one we sent at, I think, a quarter to 1.00 today. I have hard copies of the signed copy in court for everybody in Albanian and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's good to receive it. At the same time, was that on the basis of recent interviews or was it just the reworking of the former? Because what we have received, not as evidence but just to get an impression of what approximately might be led as evidence, is an interview of the 15th of May and an interview of the -- I think it's the -- of the 3rd of February, and an interview of the 5th of March, 2006. So three of this year: January, February, 15th of May, and March 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- last night I advised Chambers and the Defence that we intended to use the -- one of the statements of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- 2007. Upon reflecting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said -- I think it was said the 9th of January, but I found a combined 7th and 9th of January statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the wrong one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The date of signing is the 9th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Upon reflection this morning -- the witness arrived late, and when we managed to speak to him we combined the relevant parts from the three statements into one as a proposed 92 ter statement with nothing, absolutely nothing added to the existing three statements the Trial Chamber and the Defence have and put it together in the one package which we got -- I appreciate it was late, a quarter to 1.00. And I have hard copies -- e-mailed it to everyone at a quarter to 1.00 and had hard copies signed in Albanian and English for everyone in the court. And, I mean, to assuage any fears, it's simply -- it's just simply the three statements put together in a chronological order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. But it seems that if you have just combined the earlier statements, the last of which was from the 15th of May, that's one month ago, then I must say that 20 minutes prior to the start of court is where it's not based on new information but on just reworking this -- these old statements or all those statements is pretty late. But let's -- let's first receive them and see what we find in there. That also might have caused my confusion that Sanije Balaj was not in the 92 ter statement because I still thought that it would be the January statement that would be the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did I when I came into court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the new statement raises the problem with paragraph 85 once you receive it, because there she's specifically addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's what I said, I would not lead that last line. I understood it was just then because it was late, and I asked for it to be taken out but it stayed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I just permit myself one other observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In the covering e-mail that was sent to Chambers and to the Defence, the suggestion is made that the late service of this document is somehow connected with the late arrival of the witness, which was a suggestion that Mr. Re just repeated. With the greatest of the respect, I cannot for the life of me see how the late arrival of the witness explains the late disclosure and service of what was an unsigned witness statement. Maybe the signed version which has, I think, only just been disclosed as we've been in court today couldn't been provided, but it is simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, if I may interrupt you, I think that my reference to this being cut-and-paste from statements, the last portion of which was taken on the 15th of May, was clear enough in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, before I give you an opportunity to respond to what has been said by counsel, I'm just looking at you, Mr. Troop, whether you would like to add anything to what has been said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TROOP
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add, Your Honour, but I would adopt what Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith said and fully support their submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re, it's not entirely clear to me yet that proceedings ongoing in Kosovo, were you aware of that any earlier than when you -- well, you -- I don't remember that I've heard about it from the Prosecution. Were you aware of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. They're quite notorious proceedings. They're one of the few war crimes -- war crimes proceedings which have actually occurred in Kosovo against the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- now another question is: I do understand that the -- a body has been identified recently by DNA. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The report is dated 28th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'm trying to understand. Up till that moment there was no -- there were no remains identified as being the remains of Sanije Balaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't answer that in detail. All I can answer is that the DNA result confirmed the identity of a body that was recovered in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- September 1998 as that of hers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking myself, I don't know anything about the details of this prosecution, but if you prosecute someone for murder, for example, you usually would not engage in such a thing unless there's evidence that the person has died. So therefore, I'm just asking myself to what extent the fact that Sanije Balaj is deceased was already known earlier because it's unclear to me how you could start proceedings for, I take it, a manslaughter or murder of this woman without having evidence that she died, apart from whether it's DNA evidence or not. But has there been other evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is other evidence. Mr. Dutertre is in a much better position to explain that to the Trial Chamber than I am because he is more familiar with forensic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because what seems to be -- in view of -- and I have not studied, as a matter of fact, the request for amending the indictment there to seek leave to amend the indictment, but I take it that identifying the remains as the ones of Sanije Balaj, I take it, justifies that this, until now, unnamed victim, of which there apparently is evidence that she died but that this person died, although unnamed in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't give you the evidence in detail of what is before the court in Kosovo as to what happened to the body. I know the evidence is that there is direct evidence being led of her being shot in a forest by KLA people, being shot and buried, and that's the body. I can't give you as I stand here -- Mr. Dutertre will be able to explain in better detail the forensic evidence of where the body went and how it was recovered. What we now have is a positive DNA identification of her body as one of the unnamed bodies in the indictment found by the Lake Radonjic canal area in September 1998. That's the missing piece for this particular indictment. It -- there is some overlap, of course, with the proceedings in the Kosovo court, but we are relying upon DNA evidence to prove the identity, I think, of some 40 or so bodies, which the case in Kosovo is against one person for the murder based upon direct evidence of him shooting her in a forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you for this clarification. I'd like to give you an opportunity to respond to what Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith have raised, and of course one of the issues that might become central for the Chamber is how to proceed. I do understand that you have made a suggestion that Mr. Emmerson opposes the solution you suggest. Mr. Emmerson made a kind of a counter-proposal. Would you apart from other matters also address the solution of the present problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement of Mr. Krasniqi, the next witness, was served, that's the March 2006 statement, containing the material in relation to Sanije Balaj and her death, was served on the Defence I think in May 2006. The Defence has been on notice for a long time, as Mr. Emmerson himself acknowledged, that it was part of the Prosecution case and the general pattern about what happened to people who were suspected of being KLA collaborators. When we received the DNA report from the ICMP, which is dated the 28th of May, before we could inform the Trial Chamber and the Defence of our intention to amend the indictment, we first of all had to notify the victims -- sorry, the family and to make some further investigative inquiries in Kosovo. We were not in a position to notify the Trial Chamber or the Defence until the 6th of June. We notified them on the earliest -- at the earliest possible opportunity. Mr. Cufe Krasniqi has been on our witness list since January. His witness statements have contained the information about Sanije Balaj and we always intended to lead that evidence, and, in fact, some evidence was led and cross-examined in the evidence of Mr. Rrustem Tetaj by Mr. Emmerson himself in relation to what happened to Sanije Balaj. The accusation of her being a Serb collaborator and Prosecution case of what happened to Serb collaborators as part of the JCE has always been part of the Prosecution case here, as an example of what happened to KLA collaborators, although we did not have positive identification of a body which we could particularise in the indictment. Now, the Defence has been on notice, of course, since we provided them with the notification on the 6th of June that we were intending to amend the indictment to include the allegation or naming -- naming the unnamed victim as Sanije Balaj and they were also on notice that we were calling Mr. Cufe Krasniqi from last week. The question, why are we calling him now? The answer to these are simple. The Court has issued some 14 subpoenas to date to get our witnesses to The Hague. The Prosecutor, when she opened these proceedings, addressed Your Honours as to the difficulties we were having before trial in getting witnesses to come to The Hague for various reasons. The fact that the Trial Chamber has issued, I think, 14 subpoenas is reflective of what the Prosecutor said in her opening and the reality. And Your Honours have seen in each of the applications that we have filed, and we will probably file another one tomorrow in respect of another witness, you have seen the reasons which we have placed in the declarations of the investigators as to why witnesses do not wish or are reluctant to testify here. Mr. Cufe Krasniqi was not supposed to be the witness testifying today, first today. We had another witness who was subpoenaed and the subpoena was returnable today, but the witness has not appeared and we are attempting to have the witness come to court as soon as possible. The situation is that we are having a lot of difficulty in getting witnesses to court and in the order in which we would ideally like to call them. This particular witness, Mr. Cufe Krasniqi, who is a serving police officer, is willing, available, and ready at a relatively short notice to come to court, and we had to call him as one of the few people we could get at short notice, having a visa and being available to travel for this week. There was another witness who was supposed to have come last week and didn't appear because the subpoena had not been served. There was another witness last week who disappeared when he was supposed to be -- Mr. Kabashi, after he was cited for contempt and his evidence should have taken a few more days. The situation was Mr. Krasniqi should really have been called a little bit later but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, if I may interrupt you. I did not hear from the Defence that they were, perhaps apart from some general remarks on scheduling, that -- I didn't hear anything that would be an indication that the Defence would not see the problems that you are facing at this moment, that is, witnesses who disappear, witnesses who do not respond to subpoenas. So you spend a lot of time on that, but I think the main -- the major issue raised by the Defence at this moment is how to proceed with this witness under the present circumstances, which are to a large extent unrelated to the unavailability of other witnesses. I mean, took the criticism on to schedule this witness at this moment -- well, perhaps not be totally ununderstandable in view of the information recently received, but nevertheless that seems not to be the major issue. The major issue seems to be how can we proceed in such a way that the Defence is able to digest all the new information in such a way, including considerations of whether any additional investigations have to be done, and proceed with this witness. I think that's the core problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The suggestion is this: I just wish to correct something Mr. Emmerson said when he said that the 15th of May statement related to Sanije Balaj. It just doesn't. It's all in the statement of the -- of March last year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The suggestion I've made is that in our view, the Prosecution's submission, the evidence is severable on cross-examination in relation to Sanije Balaj. We -- the Prosecution had always intended to lead that evidence, and nothing about the application to amend the indictment changes in any way the evidence we would have led about Sanije Balaj. That remains the same. The issue is notice and cross-examination. Now, the material Mr. Emmerson seeks such as the complete UNMIK file, well the Prosecution -- we don't have the complete judicial file. The trial is ongoing, and it should be finished fairly soon. The closing submissions are due this week or next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do we have or what do you have? You say not the complete file but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have the investigation file and some of the judicial file, and we've asked UNMIK for the overlap since they provided the investigation file last year, and the judicial file. As far as I understand, we don't have the judicial file. The transcript is publicly -- publicly available and we have some of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there is a transcript of the court hearings, do I understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't -- there is, but I don't believe that we have all of it, and the case is certainly ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also do understand that it's mainly final submissions rather than hearing additional evidence that is at this moment where we stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We have requested the entire file, but as far as I know, we do not have it as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, has the -- has all this material you have, even if incomplete, has everything been disclosed and when has it been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't answer that as I stand here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can. It has not been disclosed. This is the first I've heard of Mr. Re mentioning it now. All we have, just to make it absolutely clear, and the suggestion that material in relation to this has been in the possession of the Defence for some time is again, with respect, not a fair reflection of the position. On the 25th of May, that is before the DNA results were obtained, the Prosecution disclosed to the Defence statements of the cousins of Sanije Balaj, one of them taken in 2002 and one of them taken in March 2006; in other words, they had that material in their possession but had chosen not to serve or disclose it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you, was it not in any way disclosed, not even Rule 68 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- relevant, general material.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely not, and to make matters perhaps a bit clearer, I am looking at the statement of Hazir Balaj which is contained as an appendix to the motion to amend the indictment, paragraph 3, in which the following is said: "I have given two statements to the United Nations submissions in Kosovo, UNMIK, on 21 October 2002 and 26 April 2005 concerning the disappearance of Sanije Balaj. Although the 2002 statement is handwritten, I wish to emphasise that this is not my writing. It was written by the interviewer. On 9 May 2007, I testified at the UNMIK trial of Idriz Gashi, who is accused of having murdered her. I have been shown those statements as well as the statement I gave to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in 2006." The three documents that are referred to there, the 21 October 2002, the 26 April 2005, and the testimony of 9 May 2007 have not been supplied to us. The first time I knew about them was yesterday when I received this motion. I -- as I said earlier, I have a laundry list but I did not wish to take up the Court's time with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And if I may pick it up at that point, it is perfectly clear from the service of the statements that were served on the 25th of May dating back to 2002 and 2006, that the Prosecution must have known before the receipt of the DNA report on the 28th of May that they were proposing to pursue the course of action that they have now pursued; in other words, they must have had advance notice from the ICMP, which is what has happened in the past of what the likely results were going to be, in other words, notification, because they have set in motion the process of disclosing statements that they had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They had set in process the -- set in motion the process of disclosing to the Defence statements which they had in their possession but had chosen not to disclose since this prosecution began. As Mr. Guy-Smith has just indicated, yesterday we received a selection of documents attached to the Prosecution's application to amend the indictment which make two things clear. First, and we've heard confirmation from Mr. Re just a moment ago, is that the Prosecution is currently in possession of material which it has not disclosed to the Defence; the second is that there may well be a considerable body of further material which the Prosecution is not in possession of but which is available in Kosovo. The net result is that for Mr. Re to stand here grandly saying that we've all known for some time that the next witness will say, as he will, no doubt, I've interviewed this woman for suspected collaborate and then released her and I'm innocent of any allegations of what may have taken place thereafter. It is part of the patch-work. But the reality of what actually occurred and the matters that would need to be explored in cross-examination are the material over which the Prosecution has retained exclusive control and chosen not to disclose to the Defence until, first of all, the 25th of May and then yesterday and are in continuing breach of their disclosure obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, well, what is said is -- these are hard words, and I think I'd like to focus on two questions. First, that is that additional disclosure was of material that was already - at least that's the allegation - was already in your possession for quite some time, that this additional disclosure took place just prior to the -- to the moment that the DNA identification was there. This raises some bad thoughts on the minds of the Defence. And the second is that there is still material relevant, at least likely to be relevant, to know in relation to the circumstances under which Sanije Balaj may have been killed not available to the Defence at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one in relation to the ICMP, I'm not quite sure what is meant by "bad thoughts on the part of the Defence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I hear them say - let me be quite clear - is that suddenly a new flow of disclosure took place just a couple of days before the DNA reports became available. And what the Defence suggests, that's at least how I understand it, is that you had this material for quite some time, that you have chosen not to disclose it, although they consider it to be relevant, and that in just a couple of days before the DNA report was available, you suddenly changed your mind and then disclosed it to the Defence. And as they say, that you earlier violated your obligations in not disclosing that material. That's a clear suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's just rubbish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is, it's complete rubbish. The DNA report's dated the 28th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's about the material disclosed just prior to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just about to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- it's dated the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We became aware within days of that there was likely to be a positive identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- within days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly how many days, but it's days. Now, I'm not at liberty to say how and why, but we became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So there's no conspiracy here about this -- and if we would have had this information before, we would have put it in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Look, look.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course we would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, it seems that you do not -- perhaps I misunderstand the Defence. But I do understand that the issue is that where you may have been aware a couple of days before the 28th of May that DNA identification material would become available, that at that moment you started to disclose other material, other material, that was relevant already, irrespective of the DNA findings, and that you had not disclosed any earlier, where the Defence says that this was in violation of your disclosure obligations that's any relevant material to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I fundamentally disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a coincidence that on the 25th of May additional disclosure was made?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, it relates entirely to that DNA. We had, as I've said, some information that the DNA report -- that a positive DNA report had or would be made. I can't tell you exactly when it was, but it was within days of it being dated. It was around then that we disclosed the material. Of course, the two are related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I understand is that the Defence says that any statements taken years before that were relevant already, irrespective of whether there would have been any DNA identification in May 2007, and therefore had to be disclosed already for years or at least months and that you should have disclosed that also and earlier and not to wait until there would be any DNA report. That's the allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We've got a lot of witness statements we haven't disclosed, for obvious reasons. If they're not spot-on something that's in the indictment, we normally don't disclose them. Of course it's debatable what's within Rule 66(B), but I disagree, the Prosecution disagrees with the interpretation being put forward by the Defence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also talking in terms of Rule 68 under (ii). That is not exculpatory material but the general disclosure of material that may be relevant in electronic format.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to speak across. Mr. Re has based his submissions to Your Honours today on the fact that this has always been part of the Prosecution's case on joint criminal enterprise. It may not have been a named victim in the indictment, but it has always been a part of the Prosecution's case, the Sanije Balaj incident. In disclosure batch 120 on the 25th of May they disclosed a statement from her brother dated the 15th of October, 2002, and a statement from her cousin dated the 3rd of March, 2006. Yesterday they disclosed another statement from her brother dated the 25th of April, 2006, and a statement from her cousin -- further statement from her other cousin as well. Now, the fact of the matter is that matter has been in their possession for -- in some cases just over a year and a few months and in some cases, certainly from the earliest of it, for several years. If Mr. Re is maintaining, as he does, that the incident with Sanije Balaj has always been a part of the Prosecution's case on joint criminal enterprise. It does not lie in his mouth now to stand here and say of course we are in possession of relevant material that is relevant to issues that are not mentioned on the indictment but we don't consider it part of our prosecutorial duty to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, once again, to be perfectly clear, one of the individuals whose -- we now have heard testified in the case in Kosovo was considered to be the suspect in the death of Sanije Balaj and they have statements dated, of this gentleman Avni Krasniqi, of August 2005 which is mentioned in the -- which is mentioned in their motion, September 2000, December 2002. They have further statements with regard to a gentleman by the name of Ahmet Ukaj of December 2002, April 2005, June 2005, and February 2006. And the reason that we are aware of that is because these are materials which were referred to in the testimony of these gentlemen but is also contained in their motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I understand Mr. Re to say these statements were not specifically relevant for this case because we could have sent all statements of all killing incidents in the past or people disappearing and that would have been too much, is that -- and only since the DNA identification, they became relevant. If I -- have I understood your position well?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Since she became a named victim, we had can identify her, we disclosed the surrounding material. She was part of the case in the sense that it was an incident we wish to lead evidence of, but the rest of it, because she wasn't named as a person directly in the indictment, it would appear that these weren't disclosed in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Defence has drawn --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the attention of the Chamber to what they consider to be an inconsistency in this. We'll have a look at it. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the submission just made by Mr. Re is disingenuous, at best. The entire issue of Sanije Balaj and specifically the issue of these statements has been something that has been of concern and has been discussed in a variety of different fashions, if not -- if not certainly by early this year in February, last year when I wrote a letter asking for UNMIK files specifically dealing with investigations that were going to be involved in this particular indictment. This particular issue was not an issue, and by that I mean the Sanije Balaj incident is not an issue that they in any way were going to avoid or not take a serious look at. They were going to have comprehensive information about it, they went for comprehensive information about it, they knew who the witnesses were who were involved in this particular incident, and as a matter of fact they -- the information that they've given us and the names they've given us are those incidents that they've predicated JCE upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One further matter, which is some of these individuals are percipient witnesses to the allegations that are contained with regard to the death and the matter in which -- whatever happened to Sanije Balaj's body. They are percipient witnesses, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think the best -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wants to further consider the matters raised and how to proceed and wants to take the break now, early break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered the present situation. Without having thoroughly studied the application for leave to amend the indictment and all the annexes thereto, the Chamber doesn't want to hear any evidence of the witness who will now appear on the Sanije Balaj issue. We'd first like to see that material. We also would like to give the Defence an opportunity to see that material. That means that the examination of the witness, not to say that she could not be recalled at any later stage to hear evidence from the witness on the disappearance and killing of Sanije Balaj, but at this moment the Chamber wants to limit the examination of the witness to other issues. That is one. Secondly, the Chamber would like, before the witness comes in, to identify in now the newest 92 ter statement exactly the portions -- first of all, the portions in relation to Sanije Balaj because the Chamber would like to exclude that, but I do understand that that is not in dispute. We do understand that we find in paragraph 24 -- Mr. Re, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 24. Where does that start?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 8, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but what line exactly do we start --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It will be right before paragraph 25, moving up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it just the last -- I see Hasan Gashi was stationed with his troops in the red school where Sanije Balaj was brought. Is that the first time she is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it is, but that piece of evidence is actually necessary about the red school. In our submission, it's a harmless reference whether we hear any evidence on it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any problem on these specific -- these five words where Sanije Balaj was brought?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problems in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I would like at some stage to have the opportunity to address you as to cross-examination but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if there -- there seems not to be a major problem, so we are not excluding those five words. Where then does Sanije Balaj appear again, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only other reference I can see is in paragraph 85, which is the last line, which reads: "In the case of Sanije Balaj there was an unfortunate execution without a fair trial. Such things are not supposed to happen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would then be the last sentence of paragraph 85 to be taken out. Now, I'm addressing the Defence. Any other portion where there's objection and then I take it that it's mainly about opinion, because I have not compared where in the 29, 42, 80, 81, where to find it in the new 92 ter statement, because I've just not read it. Could you tell me where to find the portions you objected to?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Re has excised the portions in the latest 92 ter statement that I objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the latest is the one we have on our desk at this moment, that is, ERN numbers last four digits 1114 up to and including 1167.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is English and original, English going until 1139.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- as I say, I haven't had the opportunity to make the specific comparisons, in part because I think the paragraph numbers no longer correspond, but I understand from Mr. Re's e-mail serving this document that he's taken the point that I made and that he has given effect to it and on that understanding that point has been addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if the witness appears and if the witness attests what he's supposed to attest under Rule 92 ter, then it's clear. Mr. Emmerson, by the way, the Chamber discussed the matter. If there would have been opinion evidence in there, of course, and I know it's in accordance with the Rules to say that that could not be admitted because it's opinion rather than facts. If it would slip in, it would not change anything for this professional Chamber. I mean they are not a jury, and it's not because the witness says, well, you see, the armed conflict started on the 3rd of the November that the Chamber would say, Well, that's the evidence, so we adopt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber would take such an opinion only if the Chamber by itself comes to a similar opinion, so concerns about that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It may have been oversensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we -- I would like to ask the Prosecution whether you're ready, Mr. Re, to call your next witness to be -- yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe that I had previously interposed an objection with regard -- and I'm just not sure about the paragraphing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: New one, 85, 86. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I previously objected to what is now 85, 86, and 87. I believe that Mr. Re indicated that he would not, because he said he received my e-mail late, that he would lead that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I said that I hadn't taken it out because I'd received it late, but I think it -- in my view, it really falls within the oversensitive type of objection. It can be led orally, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Guy-Smith, whether 85 is opinion or not, in the beginning the penalty for being a collaborator was, of course, life imprisonment, and then to say that there were no prisoners, of course you could say that's opinion, but even there I would not be that much concerned that a Chamber would adopt that it would be life imprisonment if there were no prisons, if there were no courts, let's focus on whether, for example, there was military police, yes or no, and -- so if this sufficiently meets your concerns, then we could proceed. One thing is for sure: The last line of 85 -- last line of 85, last sentence of 85, is not subject of the evidence to be given by the witness today. Mr. Re, are you ready to call Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I am ready to call Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As we are waiting for the witness, Mr. Re, may I ask, the date of this statement is today, 14th of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: -- as mentioned on page 25 in the English version, yes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll also use the opportunity, since we are waiting for the witness, of course the Chamber will more thoroughly study not only the application for leave to amend the indictment, but also the annexes to that. And if that would change our minds as far as the course to take is concerned, then of course we'll see. But we are -- at this moment we're just people that are walking in darkness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krasniqi. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Re, who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. Cufe Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's pronounced Cufe Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, Cufe Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you born on the 24th of March, 1959, in Vranoc in Peje?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And are you currently a police officer working in the training school in the KPS in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, instructor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Police instructor. And I want to show you a statement. Do you have a copy of it there in front of you? It's a statement you signed several hours ago.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have it there with you or do you -- or do you want a copy?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's here. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to make sure we're all looking at the same thing, it's Exhibit 65 ter 1384. I just want you to look at the document. Have you signed it in English and Albanian on each page, and is it dated the 14th of June, 2007?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And does this statement comprise the evidence you would give if I were to ask you questions and answers based upon everything in the statement?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is the statement -- everything in it true to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I believe it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On that basis may it be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, that would be exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit Number P351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the basis of the earlier discussions, I take it that with the exception of the last sentence of paragraph 85, there's no objection against admission. Then it is admitted, with the exception of the last sentence of paragraph 85. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some further questions, additional to some of the material there, and some clarification. Just some personal details which aren't in the statement. Did you do your JNA service in 1979 in Croatia in an anti-aircraft artillery unit before joining the police?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you first hear of Ramush Haradinaj in 1997 after his brother, Luan, was killed near the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. I heard after 1997, after his brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you first meet him in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I met him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you first meet Lahi Brahimaj in 1997 at the funeral of your cousin Adrian Krasniqi, who had also been killed?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the first time that you became [sic] of a KLA headquarters in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: For the first time, it was 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the first time you went there?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I went there for the first time after March, so after the attack on the village of Gllogjan. So I went there to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the KLA headquarters in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At those days it was not located yet. Then later it was located in a house. When I went there, it had no location yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When it became located in a house, whose house was it? Which family owned that house?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: UCK command was in the house of a relative of Haradinaj, he was a cousin of Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times did you go there in 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I went there two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the second time you went there?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The second time, I think it was after May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who did you go there with?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I went alone, with some friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember going there with Rrustem Tetaj?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I was not with Rrustem. I was with other people. Rrustem was not with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Ramush Haradinaj there when you went there?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, he was there. He was having a break. I told the people not to wake him up, and then I went, without meeting him, on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Rrustem Tetaj there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I haven't met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many people were in that building when you went there to see -- when you went there?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It was a courtyard. The doors were open. I saw some young men. There were about 70 up to 100 people, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Some were sitting, some were having a break, some were doing something, some were cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Most of them were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were any of them involved in training, military training?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I saw some people who had rifles. Somebody was explaining to them the rifles, some were talking to each other about the rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of rifles?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Usually they were Kalashnikovs, A-47.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately what percentage were in civilian clothes and what percentage were uniformed?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say because I was not interested. We would have worn such uniforms, we would have liked to have them, but we did not have such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the 70 to 80 people there, to your knowledge, KLA members? I'm sorry. I should have said 70 to 100 people, that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were there to become UCK members, but unfortunately there were no uniforms for all of them. Some of them had uniforms, some of them did not have uniforms. That was how it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about KLA patches, were the people there, 70 to 100, wearing or sporting KLA patches?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, not all of them had such patches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: I went there because we wanted to know what we could do to protect the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you elaborate a bit more on that. What do you mean by protect the village, against who? And why did you go there to get protection for your village?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Very simple. The Serbian police forces and Serbian army were attacking the unprotected villagers, the villages. It was a repression which was exercised not only that year but which had started in 1990, so probably even starting from 1989 when the constitution was changed. So that was the most difficult time for people who lived in that area. There was terror, violence. The schools were closed. The young people left because of repression because they were wanted for taking part in peaceful demonstration under charges of terrorist. So this was a daily phenomenon of the Serbian rule at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What protection were you going to get from going to KLA headquarters in Gllogjan? What were you after?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We wanted to learn about how we could do it or how can -- we wanted to learn about the routes in order to go and collect and get weapons. It was the purpose of everyone to have a weapon in his hand, to die fighting, not by being subdued, not by putting up some resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there anyone you wanted to speak to in particular when you went to Gllogjan on that second occasion?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The purpose was to discuss about setting up a group of people so that they could go to Albania to get weapons and return with weapons, carrying as much weapons as they could bear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the third time that you went to KLA headquarters in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: The third time was the worst time of that period. It was the attack on Gllogjan taking place on that day. It was a big catastrophe. The village was being bombarded from every quarter. The same thing was happening to other villages. There was shelling with heavy guns, and I could freely say then when we went there, we saw that houses were being demolished and destroyed by shelling. There were victims in civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that in August 1998?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, this was in August 1998 from the shelling of the whole region, the Serbs were making the shelling from positions in the hills. In the headquarters I met Ramush in front of the door of the headquarters. I talked to him about the situation on the ground. I told him -- asked him about the weakest point so that I could provide support with my soldiers. He explained to me that he had problems in the village of Gramaqel, Suka e Baballoq. There was Serbian positions there. There was the tank units. There are also missile systems positioned in that place. The forces of the UCK were not there in that village, Gramaqel. They were defeated. The area was plains, so the Serbs could penetrate into the village of Dubrave and in a very short -- brief period of time they could reach the village of Gllogjan.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you went there, did you have your soldiers, that is, men under your command, with you?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, I had my soldiers with me. I went with a truck. There was several soldiers with me. They were well-prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think you said in a statement of May this year that there were 27 soldiers there with you. Is that figure correct?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, the date is correct. It's also correct that I had 27 soldiers -- in fact, I had 25 soldiers and two drivers. The drivers would bring the truck back safely. We did not have good vehicles at that time, so we -- after the meeting I was instructed about the place -- the place I should go. So I went to the village of Gramaqel with the best -- with my soldiers. I was told to take position in the bridge near a stream, the stream which heads towards Baballoq.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you met Ramush in the street, was he armed and in uniform?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes, Ramush had a uniform. He did not have any rifle. He had a pistol. He -- that was close to the headquarters. He was waiting for information from the ground because there were attacks taking place from Decan, Baballoq, Crnobreg, Gramaqel, Shaptej. So the attacks were taking place in all those directions and he was there. He had nowhere to go and he was waiting for help to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he have soldiers with him?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: At that moment when I met him, he was alone. Later then, a person came. He talked to him. That person then -- I asked him where we should go so that we could attack Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know where his soldiers were when you saw him in the street?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: These were the soldiers of the village of Gramaqel, but unfortunately when I went there I did not meet anyone. I saw only five or six people on the way. There was big shelling. The Serbs were on the hills. They could see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long did you and your soldiers stay in Gllogjan for the day you're describing being under attack?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We stayed there two days and two nights. On the first day we did not take positions, we did not take the positions of guards. Then we made a small break in the village of Dubrave. These houses were near the front line, and then at about 2.00 at night, I ordered the soldiers to open some trenches because the next day would be a day of heavy fighting. So we worked during all the night. We opened a trench of about 200 metres near the bridge of Dubrave, near the bridge of Gramaqel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your men armed with? What sort of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: My men who were with me included two snipers. They had weapons of calibre M-48. I had five shoulder-launchers. I had two machine-guns of French production. I had Kalashnikovs of Russian and Chinese production.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where had you bought the machine-guns and shoulder-launchers which I think a rocket-propelled grenade is from?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We had taken these weapons from three areas. Some of them we -- were received from Albania, some from Montenegro, and some from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In your statement of May 2007 you said you bought some machine-guns and RPGs on the black market from a Yugoslav Army contact. Can you tell the Court about that?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We bought some of the Yugoslav type Zolja, they were anti-tank type of weapons. You could use them only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you bought them from within the VJ?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We bought them from officers of Yugoslav Army. These were weapons confiscated in Croatia and Bosnian and they sold these weapons to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you get the money from to buy the weapons from the enemy?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: We got the money from the peasants, they give money voluntarily without any obligation. They pooled the money. We also had relatives abroad. Everybody was ready to help the families and to provide money to get weapons so that people could protect themselves and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember how much you were paying your contacts within the VJ for machine-guns and anti-tank weapons?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: Yes. The sniper weapons which we got from the Yugoslav Army, they were in good shape and that was what we needed. We paid 1.000 up to 1.500 Deutschemarks for each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember how much you paid in total for the weaponry you had on that day from the VJ?

utterances.speaker: CUFE KRASNIQI
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. The books in which we had these figures were destroyed during the war so I cannot give you an accurate figure.
